name: Carla Kowalski

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, Carla, and thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run a continuous miner underground at a potash mine, which is the stuff they make fertiliser from. A continuous miner is a big machine with a spinning drum covered in steel picks at the front, and it cuts the ore off the face and loads it onto a conveyor behind. I'm the lead operator on my panel, so I set the pace and I'm responsible for the crew of four behind me. I'm down by seven, do the gas checks, and then I'm cutting most of the shift, with a break at the face for lunch. I like that my grandfather and my father both worked this same mine, and that I'm better at it than either of them was. What wears me out is the dust in my throat and the drive in the dark both ways in winter.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does it mean to you, working the same mine as your father and grandfather?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: It means I know who I am. My grandfather came over with nothing and the mine gave him a living, and my father raised six of us on it. Now my son Peter works three panels over. Three generations of us have breathed that dust, and not one of us ever asked the government for a thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there you go, a lot of noise about nothing, and the people selling it got rich. I'd say it at church coffee after the service. I'm not online, I don't trust it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means I keep my job, Peter keeps his, and I retire at sixty-five like I always planned. That's all I want. I've never used any of those AI things and I never will.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing changes. I keep cutting, I keep putting a little in the church plate, and I count down the years. Maybe we'd finally fix the porch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and a bit smug if I'm honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said maybe you'd fix the porch. What's money like at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Walt hurt his back underground eleven years ago and he's been on a small disability payment since, which he hates. So it's mostly my pay, and this mine pays less than the ones out west. We don't have anything put by, not really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Walt's on a disability payment. Is that different from a handout, the way you see it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's different, he broke his back for that mine. He earned it. A handout is when you're paid for nothing. Walt was paid with his spine.

S0.say: A lot of noise about nothing, and the people selling it got rich. She'd say it at church coffee after the service, not online, because she doesn't trust it.
S0.think: It means I keep my job, Peter keeps his, and I retire at sixty-five as planned. I've never used AI and I never will.
S0.do: Carries on cutting, keeps giving to the church plate and counts down to retirement. Hopes to finally fix the porch.
S0.quote: A handout is when you're paid for nothing. Walt was paid with his spine.
S0.fieldNote: Carla's identity is tied to three generations at the same mine, and to never having asked for help. She draws a firm line between earned support, like her husband's disability payment, and handouts. Her savings are thin because her husband's injury made her the main earner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the city people and the tech companies again, deciding things for places they've never seen. I'd say the government should stay out of the way and let the mines decide what works underground. At church I'd say we look after our own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it frightens me. The company already steers continuous miners from the surface at their other mine. If they bring that here, they don't need a lead operator at the face, and Peter's job goes too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working and keep my head down and not give them a reason to pick me. We'd cut back on everything, no eating out, no Christmas trip to my sister's. I'd vote for whoever says they'll protect mining jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. It's like hearing the roof work above you.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the company offered training to run the miners from the surface, would you take it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I don't think so. I'm not a screen person and I'm too old to start sitting in an office. My hands know that machine. I'm not going to learn to drive it with a mouse at fifty-eight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You're worried about Peter's job too. What would you tell him?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him to take the training if they offer it, he's young, he can do it. It feels wrong telling him to do what I won't, but it's different for him, he's got three little ones.

S1.say: It's the city people and tech companies again, deciding things for places they've never seen; the government should stay out and let the mines decide. At church she'd say they look after their own.
S1.think: It frightens me, because the company already steers continuous miners from the surface at its other mine. If that comes here, there's no need for a lead operator at the face, and Peter's job goes too.
S1.do: Keeps working and keeps her head down so she isn't picked first. Cuts eating out and the Christmas trip to her sister's, and votes for whoever promises to protect mining jobs.
S1.feel: Anxious, like hearing the roof working overhead.
S1.quote: My hands know that machine. I'm not going to learn to drive it with a mouse at fifty-eight.
S1.fieldNote: Carla blames distant city people and tech firms, while wanting government to stay out of mining decisions. She refuses surface training for herself but would urge her son to take it, and noticed the contradiction herself. Her son's young family is as much a part of her worry as her own job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is what happens when nobody puts the brakes on. I'd want the people who run this country to remember who built it. At church, I'd say we pray, and then we help each other.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Just between us, it would break me. Sixty, nothing saved, Walt on his back, and Peter out of work at the same time. I don't know how we'd keep the house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to the pastor and to my sister first, not the government, and see what the church can do for families like ours. We'd take Peter's family in if they needed it, and pool everything. I'd sell my truck and Walt's tools. I'd only go to the welfare office if there was no other way, and I'd hate every minute.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Panicked. Like being in a fall of ground with no way back to the shaft.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does it matter that there's only two years' warning, rather than five or ten?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years is nothing. With ten, I'm out on my pension and it's Peter's problem, God help him. With two years there's no ladder out. It's me, Walt and Peter's kids all under one roof on one pension.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would it be like going to the welfare office?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Shameful, for me. My mother would turn over in her grave. But I'd go if the grandkids needed feeding, because family comes before pride.

S2.say: This is what happens when nobody puts the brakes on; the people running the country should remember who built it. At church she'd say pray, then help each other.
S2.think: It would break me: sixty, nothing saved, Walt on his back, and Peter out of work at the same time. I don't know how we'd keep the house.
S2.do: Goes to the pastor and her sister before any government office and takes in her son's family if needed, pooling everything. Sells her truck and Walt's tools, and goes to welfare only if there's no other way.
S2.feel: Panicked, like being trapped by a fall of ground with no way back.
S2.quote: With two years there's no ladder out. It's me, Walt and Peter's kids all under one roof on one pension.
S2.fieldNote: The two-year picture hits Carla's whole family at once, and she has no plan beyond church, sister and pooling households. Her resistance to welfare gives way only when she pictures the grandchildren going hungry. She said plainly that family comes before pride.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough time for the companies to do it decently. Keep the old hands on until their pensions, train the young ones. That's what a decent company would do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years and I'm sixty-three. Two years short. That could mean selling the house, or it could mean the church and family carry us through. It's a real worry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put every spare bit towards the house, take every overtime shift, and Walt would look for something light he could do, maybe the hardware shop. I'd push Peter to do the surface training in year one. And I'd ask the company straight out if they'd keep the older operators until sixty-five.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be lying awake doing sums.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would five years change your mind about the training for yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I'd rather spend the five years doing what I'm good at and saving. I'd sooner give them five more good years at the face than two bad ones in front of a screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Walt say about looking for work again?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd be glad, honestly. He's hated sitting at home. His back won't let him lift, but he knows every bolt in that hardware shop better than the kid who runs it.

S3.say: Five years is enough time for the companies to do it decently: keep the old hands on to their pensions and train the young ones. That's what a decent company would do.
S3.think: Five years puts me at sixty-three, two years short of the pension. That could mean selling the house unless church and family carry us through.
S3.do: Puts every spare bit towards the house, works all the overtime and has Walt look for light work at the hardware shop. Pushes Peter to do surface training in year one and asks the company to keep older operators until sixty-five.
S3.quote: I'd sooner give them five more good years at the face than two bad ones in front of a screen.
S3.fieldNote: Five years gives Carla time to save and to get her son trained, but not to close the two-year gap to her pension. She still rejects training for herself. Her husband returning to light work came up as something he would welcome.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, so there's no excuse for the companies or anybody else. Let families and churches and the mines sort it out together. Don't wait for the government.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years and I'm sixty-eight, on my pension. But Peter will be forty-three, with kids in high school, and his job will go. And the town, all of it. I'd be safe and still worried sick about him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on and retire at sixty-five. I'd keep at Peter to get trained for something, maybe the electrical side. And I'd help get the church's men's group and women's group talking about what the town does after.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, more for my son than for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said 'the town, all of it'. What would you miss most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The Friday night fish fry at the miners' hall. Everyone's there, the old ones and the kids. If the mine goes to robots, there's no Friday fish fry, because robots don't eat fish.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want Peter to do in those ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learn a trade that needs hands and can't move away, like electrical or plumbing. And stay near his family. That's what my dad would have told him.

S4.say: Ten years is plenty, so there's no excuse for anyone. Families, churches and the mines should sort it out together rather than waiting for the government.
S4.think: By 2036 I'm sixty-eight and on my pension, but Peter will be forty-three with kids in high school and his job will go. I'd be safe and still worried sick about him.
S4.do: Carries on and retires at sixty-five. Keeps pushing Peter to train in a hands-on trade like electrical work and helps the church groups plan what the town does next.
S4.feel: Anxious, more for her son than for herself.
S4.quote: If the mine goes to robots, there's no Friday fish fry, because robots don't eat fish.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years Carla is personally safe but her worry moves to her son and the town. She sees church, families and the mine, not government, as the ones to plan the future. The Friday fish fry at the miners' hall stands in for everything she fears the town would lose.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Me, Walt and Peter all hit at once, and nothing saved. What would help is the company keeping older workers on until their pensions, and apprenticeships for the young ones so they can earn while they learn. Not welfare cheques, real work.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about faith. A lot of us down there pray before the shift. Whatever comes, I'd want the town to still have its church and its hall, because that's what holds us together.

headlineQuote: Three generations of us have breathed that dust, and not one of us ever asked the government for a thing.
portrait: Carla Kowalski is a 58-year-old lead continuous miner operator at an underground potash mine, the third generation of her family at the same mine, with her son Peter working three panels over. Her husband was injured underground, so her lower pay keeps the household and there is nothing saved. She is traditional, wary of government and city tech companies, has never used AI and won't train to run machines from the surface, though she urges her son to. Her fear rises sharply with speed, from calm in a plateau to panicked at two years, and with ten years she is safe on her pension but anxious for Peter and the town.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because she, her husband and her son would all be hit at once with nothing saved.
whatWouldHelp: The company keeping older workers on until their pensions, and apprenticeships so young people can earn while they learn, rather than welfare.
